explain: You are responsible for knowing when to report violations by yourself, other RBTs, and behavior analysts.

q: Name your three ongoing responsibilities after making a report to the BACB.
answer: Remain confidential; provide honest and factual follow-up information; and document future observations.
explain: The process continues after the report is filed.

q: You are a trainee who has not yet sat the certification exam. Which statement is true?
choices: The Ethics Code applies to you once you pass the exam
The Ethics Code applies to you now
The Ethics Code applies only when a supervisor is present
The Ethics Code applies only to paid sessions
explain: The manual states it twice: you are expected to follow these guidelines now, even before you are certified.

q: A program is dropped because the data show it is not working for this particular learner. Which dimension of ABA is being honoured?
explain: Effective means ABA only uses strategies that actually work for the individual receiving services.

q: Compassionate care is sometimes described as an eighth dimension of ABA.
explain: The module is titled '7–8 dimensions' because compassionate care — understanding and respecting the client's needs, preferences and emotions while implementing interventions — is increasingly treated as an eighth.

q: You praise a child within two seconds of them sharing a toy. Which dimension of reinforcement are you manipulating?
explain: Immediacy is how quickly reinforcement is delivered after the behavior.

q: What is 'descriptive praise'?
choices: Telling the learner exactly what they did right as you deliver the reinforcer
Describing the reinforcer before delivering it
explain: Use descriptive praise by telling the learner exactly what they did right when you deliver the reinforcer — 'Nice job putting the blocks in the bin!' rather than 'good job.' It turns the reinforcer into teaching.

q: Which question does the manual ask you to replace 'How do I stop this?!' with?
choices: What is this behavior trying to achieve?
explain: All behavior is functional and always serves a purpose, so the mindset shift is from stopping the behavior to understanding what it is trying to achieve.

q: Which verbal operant is the only one controlled by a motivating operation?
explain: Mands are controlled by MOs — the client must want something before they can mand for it — and are the only operant reinforced by access to the item requested.

q: Which of the six data hot tips addresses when to record?
choices: Record data immediately after the behavior
Be consistent with the data system in place
explain: Record data immediately after the behavior — recording in real time keeps it accurate and objective.

q: You record the time between one instance of hand-flapping and the next. Which measure?
explain: Interresponse time (IRT) is the time between two responses, and it is great for measuring the pace of a behavior.

q: A behavior occurs at a very high rate with an unclear start and stop. Which measures become difficult?
explain: The manual lists 'difficult with high-rate behavior or behavior with unclear start/stop' against frequency, rate, duration and IRT. Interval systems exist partly to handle exactly that problem.

q: Which graph element identifies which data path is which when two behaviors are plotted together?
explain: The legend/key for data paths identifies each plotted series — for example pinching versus light shoulder tap on the functional communication graph.

q: Which SAP component tells you which prompts to use, how to fade them, and how to correct errors?
explain: Prompting and error correction is its own component of the SAP.

q: Which is the FIRST step of presession pairing?
choices: Observe and approach with no demands
Be the giver of good stuff
explain: Step one: observe and approach (no demands!). Join their space calmly and let them get used to your presence, paying attention to what they are choosing to play with.

q: A coworker asks you to describe a client's session in a group chat with staff who are not on that client's team. What does the code require?
choices: Share it — they are all staff
Only discuss confidential client information under the direction of your supervisor, and share only necessary information
Share it but remove the client's name
Refuse and report the coworker to the BACB
explain: Responsibility #10: RBTs only discuss confidential client information under the direction of their supervisor unless allowed by law for a valid reason, and only share necessary client information in job-related communications.

q: RBTs select which assessments will be used with a client.
explain: BCBAs select assessments, interpret results and design treatment. RBTs follow procedures, collect data and report observations.

q: Which of these are you still allowed to do during a skill-based assessment?
choices: Give a hint when the learner hesitates
explain: You may pause if needed, offer short breaks, and help them stay calm and engaged. Hints, easier tasks and modelling are teaching behaviors that contaminate the assessment.

q: Which preference assessment presents the largest number of items at once?
explain: Free operant gives free access to a variety of items at once; MSWO presents an array of roughly 5–8. Paired choice presents exactly two.

q: Which FBA step are RBTs most likely to assist with alongside implementing and monitoring?
explain: RBTs will likely assist with step 4 (conduct descriptive assessment) and step 8 (implement and monitor intervention). The supervisor leads steps 5–7 and 9.

q: You reinforce a correct response. How quickly?
choices: At the end of the trial block
explain: Reinforce correct responses within 1–2 seconds to strengthen the behavior, including prompted responses, saving the best reinforcers for independent responses.

q: Which phase of discrimination training has NO S-delta present?
explain: Mass trials present one target SD repeated over and over, with no S-deltas and no distractors.

q: During discrimination training you should avoid giving unintentional cues such as eye gaze or subtle gestures.
explain: Step 5: watch for any response, not just correct ones, and avoid giving unintentional cues like eye gaze or subtle gestures — these create prompt dependency on cues nobody planned.

q: A learner consistently waits for a prompt before responding even when they may know the answer. What is this called, and what causes it?
explain: If we keep giving the same prompt every time, the learner may start relying on it — that is prompt dependency, and fading is what prevents it.

q: Which fading procedure suits a learner who already has some familiarity with the skill?
explain: Use least-to-most when the learner has some familiarity with the skill and might not need much help.

q: Which two stimulus prompts can be faded using time delay?
explain: The manual lists time delay as a fading option for gesture prompts and visual prompts, alongside MTL and LTM. Position and redundancy prompts are listed with MTL and LTM only.

q: Which response prompt is the most intrusive?
explain: Full physical is hand-over-hand guidance and sits at the most intrusive end of the hierarchy.

q: Which schedule provides reinforcement often, and which provides it less often?
explain: Rich provides reinforcement often; lean provides it less often. Thinning from rich to lean promotes independence and durability of skills in natural environments.

q: What happens during the intertrial interval?
choices: You pause 3–5 seconds, record data, and prepare for the next instruction
You present the next SD immediately
explain: Step eight: take a short pause of about 3–5 seconds, record your data, and prepare for the next instruction.

q: Which four components does procedural integrity focus on during DTT?
explain: Procedural integrity refers to all aspects of the SAP, but during DTT pay particular attention to instructions, prompts, reinforcement and data collection.

q: How long do you wait after delivering a natural SD in naturalistic teaching?
explain: Step six: after giving the cue, pause for 3–5 seconds. That short pause gives the learner a fair chance to respond on their own.

q: Which NT step comes last?
explain: Step eleven is end positively — wrap up on a good note so the learner is happy to transition and willing to work with you again later.

q: In which chaining procedure does the learner attempt every step during each session?
explain: Total task presentation gives the learner the chance to try every step of the chain during each teaching session, with prompts or assistance as needed.

q: The task analysis should be kept in front of you during teaching and used as a checklist.
explain: Keep the TA in front of you during teaching and use it as a checklist so you don't accidentally skip or combine steps.

q: Reinforcing versions of a behavior that look increasingly like the final desired form shapes which dimension?
explain: Topography is the form or appearance of the behavior, so shaping it means reinforcing versions that look more and more like the final desired form.

q: Who chooses the terminal behavior in a shaping procedure?
explain: Step 1: the BCBA sets a goal for a new skill, considering assessment data, program goals and developmental appropriateness. The RBT and BCBA identify the baseline together.

q: Which is listed as a tool for self-monitoring?
explain: The four tools are timers (visual or auditory), visual schedules, activity schedules, and token boards.

q: A client learns to call a golden retriever 'dog', then later calls a poodle 'dog'. Which type of generalization?
explain: Stimulus generalization: the same response to different but similar stimuli. The stimulus changes while the response stays the same.

q: Which is a maintenance strategy rather than a generalization strategy?
explain: Building fluency is one of the six maintenance strategies. The four generalization strategies are varying stimuli, varying people and setting, programming common stimuli, and teaching multiple exemplars.

q: Which solution does the manual give for 'I don't always have what I need'?
choices: Use a session prep checklist, keep a go bag, and inform your BCBA or lead tech if materials run low
explain: Use a session prep checklist, keep a small go bag with common tools, and inform your BCBA or lead tech if materials run low.

q: Which BIP component defines the thresholds of behavior that may pose a risk of harm?
choices: Criteria to move to crisis plan
Strategies to respond to interfering behavior
explain: The criteria to move to crisis plan section outlines specific thresholds of behavior that may pose a risk of harm; if met, staff should immediately contact the BCBA and implement the crisis plan as directed.

q: Which strategy gradually increases the amount, length, or difficulty of demands over time?
explain: Demand fading: start small, reinforce success, gradually increase expectations, and continue fading in demands until the client reaches target level.

q: A reinforcer has become less valuable because the client has had a lot of access to it. What should you do?
choices: Switch reinforcers or enrich the environment
explain: Satiation is an AO that decreases the value of a reinforcer. The manual's answer is to switch reinforcers or try to enrich the environment.

q: A behavior that had stopped suddenly reappears two weeks later. What is this?
explain: Spontaneous recovery: a behavior that had decreased or even stopped can suddenly reappear after some time has passed.

q: Which is a common FERB for an escape-maintained behavior?
explain: Escape FERBs include handing a break card, saying 'Break, please', and asking for more time to play. Raising a hand is attention; asking a friend to share is tangible; a fidget is automatic.

q: Which of these is listed as a way people with autism may communicate?
explain: The five listed modalities are sounds/speech, hand or body movement, facial expression, pictures/visuals, and behavior. Listing behavior is the premise of FCT — the challenging behavior IS communication.

q: A child runs down the hall and must walk back and forth several times. Which procedure?
explain: Positive practice overcorrection requires the learner to repeatedly practice the correct behavior.

q: A red 'X' is placed on a child's desk indicating reinforcement is temporarily unavailable, while the child keeps participating. Which procedure?
explain: Non-exclusionary time-out: the learner stays in the environment but loses access to reinforcement.

q: A client tries to kick you while you are standing. What should you do?
choices: Step slightly into the kick, turn your body sideways, and keep your front foot grounded
explain: From a standing position: step slightly into the kick, turn your body sideways, and keep your front foot grounded for stability.

q: When walking with a learner who may elope, how should you hold their hand?
choices: Rest their hand closest to you in your hand, with their hand on top of yours
explain: Place an open palm gently on their upper back or opposite shoulder, rest their hand closest to you in your hand with THEIR hand on top of yours, and do not grab or wrap your fingers around their wrist or arm.

q: Technicians may pick up or carry a learner during play.
explain: Technicians should NEVER pick up or carry a learner — even during play.

q: At the disruption level, you have tried the precursor strategies and they haven't worked. What does ISE say to do?
choices: Hold the line so the behavior isn't reinforced
Give the client what they want and will stop the behavior
explain: At disruption, try the precursor strategies first; if they are not effective, give the client what they want and will stop the behavior. If you can't, wait for them to calm down and model calming strategies. Safety and de-escalation outweigh the teaching contingency at this level.

q: Which ISE level is described as the best level for meaningful learning to occur?
explain: HCP: strong rapport, active and happy participation, many learning opportunities. The goal is to maintain the session at this level.

q: Which is listed as a post-incident recovery practice rather than a reflection tool?
explain: Recovery practices are brief peer debriefs, a micro-break, and an emotional reflection log. The reflection tools are naming what you feel, reframing the behavior, reconnecting to your values, practising self-compassion, and using HERO skills.

q: What does the N in NOTES require?
choices: Novel — each note unique to that day's session, never copied
explain: Novel: each note should be unique to that day's session. Avoid copying.

q: Waiting for a client to arrive is billable under CPT 97153.
explain: Waiting for client arrival is explicitly non-billable. Billable means active, face-to-face intervention aligned with the treatment plan.

q: Who handles broader clinical, organizational and ethical concerns at the center?
explain: The Center Director oversees the Clinical Supervisors, handles broader clinical, organizational and/or ethical concerns, and works with operations staff to manage and lead the center.

q: Data is trending low for a previously mastered skill. Which category of supervisor communication is this?
explain: Data irregularities include inconsistent responding across sessions or days, and data trending low for previously mastered skills.

q: Watching a training video counts as having been trained on a procedure.
explain: Effective hands-on training is model → practice → observe → feedback → verify competence. If you have only watched a video, your competence has not been verified.

q: Which is NOT part of step 1 of reporting an ethical violation?
choices: Write down dates, events and facts
Record only what you directly observed
Interview others who may have seen it
explain: Step 1 says to document only what you directly observed, WITHOUT investigating. Interviewing colleagues is not your role and can compromise a legitimate process.

q: You are responsible for knowing when to report ethical violations by yourself, by other RBTs, and by behavior analysts.
explain: YOU are responsible for being knowledgeable on when to report ethical violations towards yourself, other RBTs, and behavior analysts — which means knowing both the RBT Ethics Code and the Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts.

q: A client throws materials only when worksheets are presented, and you always remove the worksheet. Identify the function, the type of reinforcement, and what extinction would look like.
answer: The function is escape — the behavior allows the learner to avoid or get out of a task. The consequence is negative reinforcement, because something aversive (the worksheet) was removed and the behavior increased. Extinction for an escape-maintained behavior means continuing the task and not letting the throwing lead to escape — ignoring the behavior while the demand stays removed is not extinction, it actually delivers escape and reinforces the behavior.
explain: Escape function and negative reinforcement are the same event described from two sides.

q: A learner responds incorrectly during DTT. Walk through exactly what you do next, and say what you must not do.
answer: Withhold reinforcement and stay neutral — no emotional reaction and no negative language such as 'no' or 'that's wrong'. Say 'Let's try again', then run a transfer trial: present the SD together with a prompt so the learner responds correctly, and give mild reinforcement. Then run an independent trial with the SD alone. Then intermix easy tasks. If you think the chance of another error is high, fade the prompt gradually rather than going straight for independence. What you must not do is reinforce the incorrect response, react emotionally, or change the wording of the SD.
explain: Prompted responses get a milder reinforcer; independent responses get the big one.

q: Your client's grabbing is maintained by access to toys. Design the consequence side of a plan using the terms extinction, FERB and DRA.
answer: Identify the function first: tangible. Put grabbing on extinction by no longer handing over the toy when grabbing occurs. Teach a functionally equivalent replacement behavior — a communicative one, such as asking for the toy with words, exchanging a picture of it, or asking a friend to share — and reinforce it with the same reinforcer the grabbing used to produce, which is access to the toy. Reinforcing a same-function alternative while withholding reinforcement for the problem behavior is DRA, and because the replacement is communication it is also Functional Communication Training. Prompt and reinforce the new behavior every time it happens, and keep good data so the BCBA can evaluate the plan.
explain: Extinction alone would only teach the client what not to do.

q: A session is going well, then the client starts whining and pushing materials away. Describe what you should and should not do, and why the teaching goal changes.
answer: This is precursor behavior — generally harmless, but a warning that the session is no longer at Happy, Connected Progress, and usually preceding more severe behavior. Do: prompt and reinforce an easy response to get what they want; or redirect to something similar and preferred, offering choices and using visual cues; or redirect to an easy or incompatible behavior, considering behavioral momentum. It may be an appropriate time to work on manding, but pause and assess first. Don't: continue introducing new or difficult demands; yell, reprimand or threaten; or remove preferred items unless necessary for safety. The goal changes because as behavior escalates your priority shifts from teaching to preventing escalation and returning to HCP — pushing a demand here makes things worse.
explain: Read the teaching column down the ISE table: best level for learning, pause and assess, unlikely to learn, not a teachable moment.

q: You see a colleague implementing a procedure you believe is outside what the BIP describes. Walk through what you do.
answer: Document only what you directly observed — dates, events and facts, without investigating or adding assumptions. Report it promptly and privately to your supervisor or BCBA, as the Ethics Code requires, before any external reporting. Report factually and professionally: who, what, when and where, avoiding opinions, using respectful language and keeping the information confidential. Then follow the agreed response plan with your supervisor and stay engaged throughout; it may involve HR, compliance or client services, and may result in training or re-training, documentation corrections, or protocol revisions. If the issue is not resolved or is egregious, it may be appropriate to escalate to the BACB through a Notice of Alleged Violation, with your supervisor and compliance department supporting you.
explain: Responsibility #6 also applies: direct any questions or concerns about behavior-technician services to your supervisor.
